lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Part 2. You will hear a woman who makes and sells pottery giving a talk to people who want to start selling handmade goods. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: Good evening, everyone, and thanks for coming out on such a cold night. My name's Sam Ridley, and for the last nine years I've made my living selling pottery at markets and fairs.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: Before that I was an accountant, so believe me, if I can do it, so can you. Tonight I want to share some of the things I wish someone had told me at the start.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: First of all, the good news. Handmade goods are more popular now than at any time since I started. So why is that?

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: Well, it isn't the price. Let's be honest: a handmade mug usually costs more than one from a chain store, and most customers know that.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: Some sellers will tell you that handmade things last longer, too. I'm not sure that's true. A factory mug is every bit as strong as one of mine.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: What customers tell me again and again is that they love knowing exactly who made the thing they're buying. They can chat to me, ask how I glazed it, even watch me working on a piece at the stall.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: And the other reason is that no two pieces are ever exactly the same. If you buy one of my bowls, nobody else in the world has that exact bowl, and people really value that.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: Now, where should you sell? Everyone dreams of a stall at one of the big Christmas fairs, and they are busy. But the pitches can cost hundreds of pounds, and they're often booked up a year ahead.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: The large city markets are similar. There are plenty of shoppers, but there's also a lot of competition, and it's easy to get lost among two hundred other stalls.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: So for your first year, I'd really recommend school fairs. The pitches are cheap, often just ten or fifteen pounds, and parents are happy to support local makers.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: Another good option is local cafés. Many of them are glad to put your work on a shelf and just take a small share of each sale, so it costs you nothing to get started.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: As for selling online, that's something to think about later, once people know your name. On your own at the beginning, it's very hard to get noticed.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: Next, materials. When I began, I bought the most expensive clay I could find, which was a mistake, because I couldn't afford to experiment with it.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: People will also tell you to buy in bulk to save money, but you can end up with a garage full of things you never use.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: What really worked for me was joining up with two other potters and placing one big order together. We split the delivery cost, and we still got the trade price.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: Then there's the stall itself. Some sellers pile everything onto the table so shoppers can see the full range, but it just looks messy, and people walk past.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: I also used to put my most expensive pieces right at the front, and I noticed customers were nervous about picking them up.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: What really makes a difference is height. Put some pieces up on wooden boxes or little shelves, so that people can see them from the other side of the hall.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Now look at questions 17 to 20.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: Of course, things will go wrong from time to time. Every business has problems, so let me tell you about a few makers I know.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: Fern and Thread sell embroidered cushions and bags. At one fair they were next to another embroidery stall, but that wasn't really the issue.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: The real problem was that they charged far too little. When they added up the hours each cushion took, they were earning about two pounds an hour.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: Oakline started out making wooden chairs and small tables, which were beautiful. But they were so heavy that the owners had to hire a van for every single market, so now they only make toys and chopping boards.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: The couple who run the Little Wax Company make candles. At their first big fair, people kept asking if they could pay by card, and luckily they'd bought a card reader the week before.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: But by eleven in the morning they had sold every candle on the table, and they had to spend the rest of the day just giving out business cards.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: And finally, Tide Prints, who sell prints of seaside paintings. They chose a fair on a clifftop in October, and a strong wind blew half their prints into the sea. The rest were ruined by the rain.

lines.speaker: SAM
lines.text: So the lesson there is: always check the forecast and take weights and plastic covers. Right, I think that's enough bad news. Let's take a short break, and then I'll answer your questions.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: That is the end of Part 2.
